But in the “systematic” or “deductive” presentation of knowledge that has already been established, the philosopher follows the opposite order.
Within the system, the Phenomenology should therefore occupy the third and final place, after Ontology and Cosmology.

Beginning with the concept of being as such and describing its structure in Ontology, the philosopher must arrive at the concept of the existence of this being in concrete actuality—that is, at the natural and human world, or Nature and Humanity.
He describes these in the two parts of his Cosmology.
He begins with the natural world and then reaches the historical development of the human world, describing the real dialectic in the second part of Cosmology.
In this way he arrives at the historical emergence of the philosophical system that describes all of this—in other words, at his own emergence.
And having reached this absolutely concrete reality, he describes it too.
But because this reality, precisely in its concreteness, “reveals” itself to itself as a “phenomenon,” this final description by the philosopher is phenomenological in character.
The Phenomenology, as the third and final part of the system, begins with the fact that the Philosopher exists and describes the concrete content of his consciousness.
That consciousness includes the understanding of all the ways in which the cosmos “appears” to humanity.
And the Phenomenology shows that such an “integral” consciousness makes it possible to give a complete answer to the question of the structure of the being that “appears” to human beings.
For being does in fact “appear” to humanity through the philosopher’s consciousness, and the Ontology with which the system begins provides the answer to that question.
In other words, when the philosopher reaches the end of the presentation of his system, he brings the reader back once more to its beginning.
In doing so, he shows that his system is true because it is circular.
From a logical point of view, there is no doubt that this third and final place given to the Phenomenology within the system is fully justified.
With this structure, the system is logically homogeneous.

Its development begins with what is most abstract—being in general—and moves continuously toward what is most concrete: the content of the real consciousness of a living human being, namely the consciousness of the philosopher himself.
The description of this consciousness concludes the Phenomenology and therefore the system as a whole.
This position of the Phenomenology within the system would also provide several “technical” advantages for its presentation.
First, it would allow us to avoid introducing into the Phenomenology the “axioms” we discussed earlier.

The prehuman or natural foundations of human existence—which our present Phenomenology can only list without being able to explain their origin or nature—would already have been described and “derived” in natural Cosmology.
A Phenomenology placed at the end of the system could therefore refer back to that derivation.

It would not have to ask the reader to accept anything “on faith,” that is, without proof: for example, that human beings possess an animal body inseparable from them, that they live within the natural world and interact with it, that they are finite and mortal, and so on.

Second, by starting from the fact—already “derived” in historical Cosmology—that the Philosopher exists, the Phenomenology could immediately refer to the existence of a distinction between the philosophical and non-philosophical points of view.

That is, it could begin from the distinction between the point of view of the consciousnesses corresponding to the “appearances” being described and the point of view of the philosopher’s or phenomenologist’s consciousness that describes them—the “for us.”
Our present Phenomenology uses this distinction from the beginning and therefore presupposes it.

But it can prove and explain the existence of the distinction only at the very end, when it describes for the first time the consciousness that has constantly stood opposite the consciousnesses being described precisely because it is the consciousness describing them.
In that sense, everything said in the Phenomenology “in the author’s own name” is itself accepted, to some extent, on faith.
It is justified only at the end of the Phenomenology—or, more exactly, only by the Phenomenology as a whole.
Finally, third, placing the Phenomenology at the end of the system would allow us to avoid all the unavoidable repetition that occurs when the system is presented by beginning with it.

Since everything needed to describe and understand cosmological and ontological phenomena would already be known to the reader, there would be no need to dwell on those points in the Phenomenology, still less to repeat things that had already been said in Ontology and Cosmology.
All of this is certainly correct.
And yet, for what we might call pedagogical reasons, the presentation of the system as a whole must nevertheless begin with the Phenomenology.

As we know, the Phenomenology describes the “appearances” of being and therefore serves as the necessary introduction to the description of being itself and of its real existence—that is, as the introduction to Ontology and Cosmology, or to Philosophy and the system in the strict sense.
The philosopher himself was able to arrive at his Cosmology and Ontology only through an investigation of phenomena as such.
The reader likewise cannot fully absorb and master the systematic presentation of Philosophy—which proceeds from Ontology to Cosmology—without first becoming familiar with the Phenomenology.
For pedagogical reasons, then, the presentation of the system of concrete knowledge necessarily divides into two basic parts.
The first is the introductory part called the Phenomenology.
The second can be called the System of Philosophy in the strict sense, beginning with Ontology and ending with Cosmology.

Indeed, after reading the System of Philosophy, one may understand perfectly well what the “philosophical” point of view—the “for us”—actually is: the point of view from which the Phenomenology is written from beginning to end.
But the origin of that point of view would remain completely obscure.

The “philosophical” point of view, unlike that of the “scientist” or the “ordinary person,” is characterized by distinguishing the appearance from the reality that “appears”—that is, from existence—and then distinguishing that existence from being as such, the being that underlies it.

But in describing being and existence, Philosophy does not explain how or why a human being—and in particular its author—ever arrived at this “counterintuitive” distinction and this “unusual” way of posing the problem.

Only the Phenomenology shows how and why a person who begins from an “ordinary” or “natural” consciousness—which does not distinguish an “appearance” from its existence or its being—eventually and necessarily arrives at the purely philosophical question of the “causes” or “conditions of possibility” of appearance as appearance.
That is, it shows how one arrives at the cosmological and ontological questions of existence and being as distinct from appearance.

A reader without philosophical training can therefore profitably begin the study of Philosophy proper only by first passing through the phenomenological school—that is, by beginning the study of the system with the Phenomenology.

But as I have already said, presenting the Phenomenology as the first, introductory part of the system, although pedagogically justified, necessarily creates systematic and structural difficulties and makes the presentation logically imperfect.
First, we are forced to begin the presentation of the Phenomenology with unproved “cosmological” assertions.
Within the Phenomenology they remain unproved all the way to the end.
Obviously, this does not help make the phenomenological presentation itself fully convincing, nor the anthropological conclusions derived from it.

Second, as we will see, every properly philosophical description of a given “appearance,” even when it seems to be made from the point of view of the corresponding “consciousness,” is framed by a series of arguments consisting of an introduction and a conclusion.
These arguments are made from the author’s own point of view and explain what the appearance in question is “for us” or “in itself”—that is, what it is “in truth.”
The Phenomenology as a whole certainly justifies these arguments, because everything said in such introductions or conclusions eventually appears within one of the consciousnesses being described.
But at first these arguments can seem artificial and unjustified—in other words, arbitrary.
They can therefore put the reader off and lead him to stop reading before reaching the end.
Yet reaching the end means becoming acquainted with the work as a whole, and only knowledge of that whole can justify the author’s arguments.
A reader may therefore fail to complete a first reading precisely because the Phenomenology, although itself an Introduction to Philosophy, becomes fully convincing only on a second reading.
Finally, third, if the system begins with the Phenomenology, repetition becomes unavoidable.
The author is forced to say in advance, within the Phenomenology, some of what he will later have to repeat in Cosmology and Ontology.

Whenever the author speaks from his own point of view, he cannot speak only about a given phenomenon as phenomenon without also touching on the real “existence” that “appears” in this phenomenon to the corresponding consciousness—and sometimes also the being underlying that existence.
Of course, for a reader who does not yet know the Cosmology and Ontology, these cosmological and ontological “digressions” will not feel like repetitions.
But the danger is not that they will bore the reader.
The real danger is that they will mislead him and cause him to misunderstand what he is reading.

This form of presentation undoubtedly creates that risk because it cannot clearly separate a properly phenomenological description from a cosmological or ontological analysis of what is being described.
The author must do everything possible to stop the reader from falling into the trap of confusing appearances as such with aspects of existence and being.
Even so, only a reader who pays complete attention to the text will be able to avoid this confusion entirely.
For all these reasons, a Phenomenology placed before Ontology and Cosmology almost inevitably has to be read twice.
That is an undeniable disadvantage of this mode of presentation.

Nevertheless, despite this defect, philosophical and pedagogical considerations still require us, first, to treat it as the opening or introductory part of the system as a whole and, second, to read it before studying Philosophy in the strict sense.
2. The three fundamental parts of Phenomenology
The Phenomenology presented here as an Introduction to Philosophy necessarily and naturally divides into two basic parts.
But we will now see that its first part appears only because it comes before Ontology and Cosmology instead of after them.
Its third part, meanwhile, can—and must—exist only within a “socialist” Phenomenology. It has no place in a definitive or “communist” Phenomenology.
Only the second part of the Phenomenology, therefore, is directly and properly “phenomenological.”
That is why, in our work on this philosophical discipline, the second part is both logically central and fundamental, and also much larger than the others.
Let us now examine the distinctive character of these three basic parts of the Phenomenology.
I have called the first part “The Prehistorical Foundations of the Appearances of Human Existence.”
This part brings together everything without which it would be impossible either to present or to understand the second, properly phenomenological part.
At a certain level, however, this first part really belongs to Cosmology and, in part, even to Ontology—as do, for example, some of the reflections on negativity, identity, and so on.
Nature and humanity “appear” only to a concrete, living human being.
And every concrete, living human being is in fact always historical: he exists within the general dialectical development of existence that we call the “universal history of humanity.”
“Prehistorical” existence is therefore, in a certain sense, also “prehuman,” and consequently “prephenomenological.”
The prehistorical moments or aspects may in some way be “given” to the author of a Phenomenology insofar as he is a philosopher.
But they do not “appear” to the concrete, non-philosophical consciousness being described—that is, to the human being actively creating History and thereby also creating himself.
More than that: the “appearances” described in the first part not only appear to no one; strictly speaking, they have never existed anywhere in the form in which they are described.
And the dialectical process said to connect these appearances has likewise never existed anywhere in this pure form.
The first part discusses desire, struggle, sensation, master, slave, and so on.
Each “appearance” is described in isolation, or as we might say, “in pure form,” as though it existed by itself independently of every other appearance.
But it is perfectly obvious that no real, concrete being has ever been or could ever be the embodiment of desire alone, or perception alone, and so on.
Likewise, no living human being has ever been or could ever be only a master or only a slave.
Desire certainly exists in human beings, as do the other elements, and therefore “appears” to them insofar as they are conscious of it and insofar as it forms part of their self-consciousness.
And there is no doubt that living human beings really can be slaves and so on.
But desire is real only in a person in whom many other things are also taking place.

So if desire “appears” to a person, it does not appear to someone who is realizing nothing but desire. It appears to a concrete, living human being in whom other aspects and dimensions of human existence are also being realized and to whom they also “appear.”
The same is true, for example, of a real slave.
He is never only a slave. He also possesses characteristics belonging to the “human kind,” characteristics found in masters and citizens as well.
If he appears to himself and to others as a slave, he never appears as a slave in “pure form.”
He appears as “above all a slave,” or “primarily a slave,” and so on.
